utterances.text: But I think it's -- if -- it would be preferred if there would be a not underlined copy available.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, we are referring to item 102.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I underlined certain things.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Everyone has underlined some parts. If you put your copy, page 49 of the English version, on the -- on the ELMO so that we can -- I take it, General Radinovic, that the underlinings are yours?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In my copy, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, could you please point to item 102. That's 112. There we are. Thank you. Here you mentioned six strategic and military objectives. And my question is as follows: According to your experience as a general, according to the knowledge that you have of the events, are these legitimate objectives?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. I would now like to turn to the issue of what is sometimes called blockade, but I would like to ask you a question about the blockade imposed on the troops, the fact that an attempt was made to block troops in the city, this procedure, according to military strategy and doctrine, is it a legitimate procedure; yes or no?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Witness, let's turn to this issue of strategy, since we have objectives listed in six items here. Did you ever find a single document which mentioned a seventh item, the existence of a corps plan, perhaps, that would have referred to the destruction of Sarajevo and/or the elimination of the Muslim population of Sarajevo? And of course I am talking about a Serbian plan.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Witness, I would like you to specify for which reasons - because that's the sense of your report - why do you assess that the city itself, not as a source of soldiers but as a place of residence for civilians, why was this city not a city under siege, according to your experience, on the basis of your experience and your report?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: For several reasons. There are several reasons for this claim. The first - and I think this is the main reason - is that about 2 and a half kilometres, in that area, around Sarajevo was totally free, so the entire area of the Sarajevo airport was free. It was an open area. Throughout the wartime period, the Sarajevo airport was open, it functioned for humanitarian deliveries, for international meetings. The humanitarian convoys were able to come through, convoys belonging to the humanitarian agencies, the so-called blue routes were also open, and throughout the wartime period a large number of international organisations and international representations were present in Sarajevo: The UNPROFOR command, the international organisation committee. So in brief it was possible to enter and leave Sarajevo; naturally, under supervision. But the UNPROFOR commander from January 1994 to January 1995 was General Michael Rose and in his book he was quite explicit. He said that Sarajevo was not encircled and it wasn't under siege, and there was no reason not to believe the commander of the forces who had the situation in Sarajevo under their control, and this is an elite officer of the British army who was certainly familiar with the situation in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, when you say that Sarajevo was not under siege, which Sarajevo are you referring to? Because I think there is a distinction to be made there.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I say Sarajevo, I'm referring to the entire city of Sarajevo. I'm not referring to part of Sarajevo. I'm referring to the entire city. Part of Sarajevo in the strict urban sense includes Grbavica, Nedzarici, Ilidza, Rajlovac, Vogosca. These were also parts of Sarajevo, so --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'll stop you there. With regard to these areas that you have mentioned, were you able to observe anything with regard to the difficulties of the civilian population in these areas, Nedzarici, Ilidza, et cetera, in comparison to the difficulties that the population on the other side of the line had? Were you able to compare this?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wasn't there, so I was not able to experience this directly, but when I saw the state the buildings were in and having spoken to the people who lived in these buildings, I think that the difficulties and the fear of war, I think that those in Grbavica and Nedzarici were equally exposed to it as those who were in Velesici or in Alipasino Polje or in Dolac Malta, or Otok, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And would you include the possibility of physical circulation?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as far as the possibility of circulating is concerned, the people in Grbavica, they were connected to the part under the control of Sarajevo and it was easy for them to move. The people from Nedzarici, it wasn't easier for them to move than for civilians from Sarajevo. So these are parts that were under the control of sides in the conflict. Sarajevo was a divided city. It wasn't a city that had been blockaded, that was under siege. Each side had a certain part -- had its own part under its control.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. General, I would now like to move on to a delicate issue, that of casualties, the loss of life. Are you aware of a text that is called "The Tabeau report"; yes or no?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I'm not a demographer, so I'm not familiar with the fact that is a demographer would be familiar with, but yes, I have examined it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Rest assured, General, we aren't either. But were you able to come across figures regarding the losses suffered on the other side of the line? That's my first question. Yes or no?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Objection. The witness has indicated he's not a demographer, and the next witness to be called by the Defence is, in fact, an expert in this subject.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I do understand that the question was about figures, so rather about facts than to the expertise. And if a -- even if an expert would have by any chance any knowledge of certain facts, he can be asked about it. Please proceed, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, if you came across these figures, what can you tell us about the number of losses, the magnitude of the losses, during the period we are interested in on the Serbian side?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I noticed that on the Serbian side there are about 2.300 dead and there were about 3.300 dead on the other side. I'm not sure that these figures have been correctly interpreted, that I have interpreted them correctly, but this shows that there are no huge differences in the number of dead on both sides. So both sides suffered the terrors of war.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where did these figures that you obtained come from, General, the figures that you are talking about now?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I found them in the report made by Ewa Tabeau.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm talking about the other side.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this is from the Dayton documents that I had from the SRK, the Sarajevo Romanija Corps.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. So you yourself found these figures in the course of your work.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. General, could you now tell us briefly something about what the Defence calls "total war." You told us yesterday and today that there was a desire for peace expressed by General Galic himself but also by the Serbian side to get out of the impasse. What can you tell us on the basis of your experience, your report, about the attitude of the enemy side with regard to peace or continuing with the war?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: The Prosecution objects on the grounds of relevance, lack of foundation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Mr. President, this witness examined about 5.000 documents. Some of them have to do with peace agreements and others, as we have seen, concern spreading panic among the civilians on the Serbian side and they have to do with persecuting Chetniks. We saw this document a minute ago. We think that this witness may have seen other documents --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The objection is denied. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, could you please answer this question.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I examined the basic documents that have to do with the behaviour of the sides - and I'm talking about their original documents but also secondary documents, studies carried out by people who were involved in that conflict that we call the war in Bosnia and Herzegovina - when I examined these documents, I found out that from the very beginning it suited the Serbian side to negotiate peace as soon as possible, and it is my personal belief, since I was familiar with the political events, I knew that the Serbian side didn't want a conflict, but since there was a conflict, the Serbian side wanted the war to come to an end as soon as possible. But on the basis of the documents and the behaviour I observed and the sources, I gained the impression that the presidency side did not want the war to come to an end until they managed to attain their strategic objectives, and their strategic objective was defined in their documents, in their programmes, as being a single Bosnia. It wasn't to be divided. It was to be a unitarian Bosnia, and the rights of the peoples were to be respected.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, a purely technical question: Sometimes we have the impression when we examine the documents that we call SITREPs, UN reports, reports made by UN observers, we sometimes gain the impression that there is an apparent disproportion between some of the outgoing shells, some of the shells fired from Sarajevo, and others coming into Sarajevo, the part of Sarajevo under the control of the Muslim forces. My question is as follows. And the first part of my question is: How many shells have to be fired in order to attempt to eliminate an object, neutralise an object, in general? And then, the second part of my question is: What can you tell us about the observation conditions in the field for the UN observers? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as the criteria for neutralising certain targets is concerned, according to the military rules in force for certain weapons, there are norms, there are rules which specify the number of projectiles that have to be fired at a certain target in order to neutralise it, in order to attain a certain degree of neutralisation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: A specific example, please. If, for example, I am to destroy a battery that is opening fire at me, how many projectiles would I have to fire?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If the target is in the open, it's not sheltered, from a 120-millimetre mortar, it's necessary to fire 26 shells at each target in order to have -- in order to neutralise it to a 25-per cent degree. So to be -- so to have the certainty of 25 per cent of neutralising the target.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And to attain 100 per cent, do I have to multiply it by 4?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we don't know how many shells should be fired to attain 100 per cent degree of certainty. But for 50 per cent of certainty, 96 shells have to be fired at one target if it is sheltered.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, and if the object is protected?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Then even more. If it's protected, then it's not possible to destroy it. It's only possible to control it by opening fire.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, what are the sources? You say you need a certain number of shells. Could you give us a reference, a technical reference.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. You have instructions for artillery. These are instructions for 82-millimetre mortars and you have instructions for 120-millimetre mortars, and the instructions there are the criteria and the rules for the number of shell that is have to be fired to neutralise a certain target.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And who wrote these instructions, who published these instructions? Is there an institution?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, these are the official rules which are in use in the JNA -- which were in use in the JNA and are still in use in the Army of Yugoslavia today.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And as an expert, you can confirm this information; yes or no?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. General, what is the legal responsibility of a commander against whom fire might be opened? That is to say, if fire is opened against his men, if he does not -- I'm talking about a commander who does not respond to fire.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He has the professional obligation of opening -- of responding to fire and disabling the enemy, preventing the enemy from inflicting losses. So it is his duty in the system of command to take such action. But what his legal responsibility is, I don't know. I'm not a lawyer, but I assume that he has to return -- he has to be held responsible. If he has to be held responsible professionally, he has to be held responsible legally too.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, I'm going to turn to the second part of my question again, that you haven't dealt with, and it is as follows: What are the difficulties for an observer, whoever that observer may be, in a city such as Sarajevo, in order to hear the fires -- the shots being fired from the city, if these are small mortar shells, 120-millimetre shells?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if on the Papa side in Sarajevo, the BH army side, you consider that there were between five and seven observation posts - and I personally came to the conclusion that there were very few observation posts for such a large area - if one wanted to be certain of identifying all the shots, that was one of the problems. But the second problem was that when you have a densely inhabited city, it is very difficult especially if shots are being fired from behind buildings, it's very difficult to hear every shot. And this is not the case with the explosions, when the shot is already fired, you hear the explosion better than the shot being fired itself. There's a difference in the data in the observer's reports with regard to the outgoing and incoming fire.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin, perhaps this is not necessary, but I remind you that there are ten minutes left. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I think we'll manage.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, my question is: You were able to examine some documents about the media when writing your report; yes or no?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. What can you tell us, very briefly, about the conclusions you were able to reach in relation to the issue of the way the media treated information in the course of this war? And I'm referring in particular to the alleged random shelling, indiscriminate shelling. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it was my belief that the media was used as a means of war in Sarajevo, not only because they didn't understand the situation but also because they were frequently manipulated. I'll provide you with some of the most striking examples that one can show that manipulation was at stake. On the map I showed you that the claim -- that the Sarajevo Romanija Corps had all the elevated positions in -- around Sarajevo, I said that this was not true. In the media and TV reports and in the papers, and unfortunately in the official reports of UNMO teams, it says that members of the SRK surrounded Sarajevo, they held elevations around Sarajevo, and they shelled Sarajevo. This is quite simply false. And furthermore, in the UNMO reports and also in the media, they constantly mentioned the fact that it was impossible to accept the action of SRK artillery behind the front lines, and if anyone -- if you know anything about the army, you will know that the artillery is not used at the front line because in such a case you would inflict losses on your own forces. It's used in the depth, in order to attack the reserves, the firing positions of the artillery, manoeuvring forces, the movement of forces, et cetera. But it's not for forces at the front line.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, I'll stop you there. I have four more questions, and I would like to address them all. My first question is: You established that the tanks -- or almost all the tanks of the SRK were buried around Sarajevo. Does that show that there was the desire -- they were entrenched around Sarajevo. Does that show that they wanted to carry out an aggression?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. That's the least favourable way of using armoured forces. The tank has force because it unites fire, movement, and strikes, and the SRK used tanks in a way that took advantage only of its firing power, so the tank was entrenched, or rather, it was a fixed firing position, so it wasn't as effective as any cannon.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. General, the depth of the front -- I'm not talking about the zone of responsibility. I'm talking about the area which adjoining the front and where you have the various echelons of function: The line itself, then while logistics and reserve, right down to the command of the front. What is the depth of this zone in military terms, in terms of metres? How many hundreds of metres were they?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: For a battalion, it's between 3 and 5 kilometres. For a brigade, it's 15 to 20 kilometres. For a corps, it's 50 kilometres. But in an urban area, these dimensions reduced. So for a battalion, it would be 1 and a half to 3 kilometres. For a brigade, about 5 kilometres.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. General, when one uses a shell, do you know whether there is a margin of error, a technical margin of error which is related to the weapon that is used?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There is a so-called deviation of the shot, when the shots don't hit the target, they disperse.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What is the possible margin of error?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, up to 300, 500 metres. It depends on the charge. I don't really know exactly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you tell us - because I have another two questions to put to you - could you briefly tell us why this disproportion -- you spoke about snipers in your report. Why was there this difference between the Muslim position with regard to professional snipers and the Serbian position? So why was there this lack of balance?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, first of all, the 1st Corps had far more men in Sarajevo than the SRK. And since the formations were similar, one to two snipers in a detachment, well, by definition the 1st Corps had more snipers and the 1st Corps had sniper weapons that were better than those of the SRK. They had 12.7-millimetre snipers. The 1st Corps had these weapons and the SRK didn't. And the Zrak factory was under the control of the 1st Corps, and throughout the wartime period they produced equipment for the needs of the 1st Corps.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, could you tell us very briefly - and this is something that appears in your report - could you tell us why the forces in Sarajevo refused, according to your report, the possibility of demilitarising Sarajevo itself? I'm not talking about the removal of weapons. I'm talking about demilitarisation.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, demilitarisation was the only real method that could be used to avoid the catastrophes of war in Sarajevo. It wasn't accepted unfortunately, and I personally think that the Muslim side needed Sarajevo as a victim of Serbian aggression in order to attain its radical objectives, and that was to control the entire area of Bosnia-Herzegovina. It was not able to achieve this goal by using strategic means. So they were trying to cause NATO to intervene, and General Rose talks about this.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Mr. President, I think that my colleague would like us to provide a certain number of documents to the witness. These are the documents that the registrar -- Madam Registrar should already have. And the numbers, I can tell you what they are, 227, 205, 261, 263, 262, 206, 1866, 1867, 260, 254, 255, and 248. We would simply like the witness to have a look at these documents. I think that they were bundles that were already provided in order to facilitate the registrar's work.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And could the witness just tell us whether he has seen these documents by saying yes or no. Could he just tell us whether he recognises them. And we will then have other documents that we will provide directly. I think that there is -- that we have them here. I believe, yes, that we have an agreement about this. General, do you recognise these documents?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I have seen all of them. I studied all of them, and I think I quoted most of them in my report. The documents relate to the conduct of the SRK towards the UNPROFOR.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, my very last question, because I'm going to stop here, has to do with the alterations that the witness wanted to make in his reports.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, did these alterations have to do with the essence or were they simply for clarification, like the one you just mentioned, or did you want to correct misprints, typos, et cetera?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wanted to correct things that could cause translation errors.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just one question about this --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, there is one interpretation problem that I was able to identify, if I can correct it by asking the witness. And it's a formal question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous interpretation continues] ... We'll see whether we allow the witness to answer that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, don't answer immediately. Is it true that I told you when we were working together on this file that there is a spot in the English version dealing with the destruction of a neighbourhood close to what is called Ciglane and that you told me, "I didn't use the term 'destruction' in Serbian but a term that corresponds, rather, to 'damage'"? Don't answer immediately.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, you may answer the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I answer? Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. We'll deal with the other documents according to the accepted formula.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I tried to check the documents just shown to the witness, Mr. Piletta-Zanin, because we still have to deal with the unnumbered version. Could perhaps ...

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Do you want me to quote again the numbers of these documents, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous interpretation continues] ... On my screen, but I would like to have on the ELMO the document 1866 so that we can compare whether this is -- I think the matter -- this one has been clarified. That's the document that was the 7th of May, 1994. When I -- 227, could that please be put on the ELMO. Yes. Thank you. And 205, please. Yes. Thank you very much. Is the Prosecution ready to start the cross-examination of the expert witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. But first just two matters for the record.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You wanted to --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I wanted, in order to facilitate the Prosecution's work, I don't know if you want us to communicate now the documents that I referred to at the end of my questioning or during the break. It's just a question of courtesy, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. President, presumably my learned colleague is referring to documents that they're intending on tendering from the bar table. The Prosecution would be pleased at the break to receive an indication as to which documents that might be, but we have made our position clear that with respect to those SRK documents for which we have questions regarding authenticity, that we will not accept those documents being tendered from the bar table.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Is it tendering from the bar table that you intend, or were you referring to the last documents, 227, 205 --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no, Your Honour. I was referring to the last topic of my intervention, namely tendering from the bar table. And I think there is one document we could submit immediately. Not the numbers that I just listed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then I take it that the numbers will be given to the Prosecution so that they can find their position. Before giving you an opportunity to start with the cross-examination, Mr. Mundis, I would have one question to you: This map you made with all the positions on it, you remember the map that's D1913, when did you prepare that map?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I brought it with me, when I came here. When I came to The Hague, I brought it with me. That means I made it perhaps 15, 20 days ago, maybe a month ago, but I studied the documents much earlier.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Was the map made on request of the Defence or did you ...?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. That was at my own initiative.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you very much. Please proceed, Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. President, last week you also loaned the witness a dictaphone recording machine, and we have yet to receive any changes that the witness may have made.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Could -- perhaps -- I gave you my dictaphone. Are you -- have you finished whatever you'd like to do with it, or -- and what is the result of your work?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. I have completed all the work I wanted to using your dictaphone. I recorded what I had written, and I also have it on paper. I can provide the paper if required. So there are three things that I think should be borne in mind when using my report. And when you gave me this dictaphone, you said please return it. I didn't respond immediately because I thought you were joking and I still think you were, because since this is on the transcript, please tell me why did you warn me to return it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Because it's the -- it's the Dictaphone I use personally, so I'd rather continue using it in the future. That's the reason why I asked you to return it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You didn't really think that I wouldn't have returned it without that warning. It goes without saying, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous interpretation continues] ... Of course it goes without saying. I -- but the only reason is that usually if any piece of -- whether it's a Dictaphone or a computer, it's always very precisely registered. That's the bureaucracy in the United Nations. And I just gave it to you and I said I expected that you return it. There was no -- not one second thought involved in it. Yes. Mr. Mundis -- Perhaps you could, whatever you have in writing or on tape, you could please give it to Madam Usher. She'll then give it to the registry so that it will be made available for the parties. Madam Usher, could you please. Yes, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the witness just said there were three matters that need to be borne in mind. I don't know. Do you think it's good for him to enumerate them so that we have them on record?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I thought he said he also had it on paper.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. But I would prefer it to be on record, on the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Could you tell us what three matters should be borne in mind, just briefly.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, the first has to do with a possible wrong understanding of my position regarding the identities of soldiers and positions, paragraph 220. I said there is full identity of civilians and soldiers. It has to be borne in mind that I meant able-bodied men of military age, that is, from 18 to 60. Not all civilians, therefore, but only the male population in the military age -- of military age. The second thing has to do with paragraph 273 of my report, where I used the Serbian word that means "the neighbourhood of Ciglane suffered." It was translated, I was told, as "destroyed." The meaning, however, is different from the translation. What was meant was that consequences were suffered by this neighbourhood, not that it was completely destroyed. And the last correction would be to the chapter "Conclusions," conclusion number 33. I wrote that General Galic was accused of holding Sarajevo under siege. I used the wrong term because I was carried away by the allegations made in the accompanying documents, which said that General Galic was accused of terrorising civilians by shelling and sniping during siege. So I made this slight of hand, and I'm sorry I wrote this. I would kindly ask you to bear in mind that I meant the allegation regarding the terrorising of the population by shelling and sniping from the position of siege. And the last remark: I'm not sure that there are no misprints, changing the number of an item or the date which would reflect on the document they used for this particular claim. But if there are such mistakes, I will find them and correct them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That is clear, General Radinovic. Mr. Mundis, then please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Cross-examined by Mr. Mundis:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, your Ph.D. is in political science. Can you tell us what the title of your dissertation was.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My dissertation was not in the area of political sciences. It is titled "The method of military science." So it's a question of methodology of research in military science.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You've testified here at the Tribunal in two previous cases, the Foca and Krstic cases; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And in those trials, just as in the present case, you prepared a report and testified under oath; is that right?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Page 202 of your report in the English version there's a list of books that you referred to. Can you please give us the titles and authors of any other books that you may have consulted in preparing your report..

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't understand the question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Other than the books listed --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, objection. I don't have page 202 in my copy of the report. Maybe I'm more modest than others, but I have a copy that ends with 195. Maybe we're talking about a different report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. President, on the version of the report filed with the registry, in the lower right-hand corner, immediately prior to the witness's CV is the number "202". At the top of that page, it says "Studies and books."

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed. So the question was whether you did consult any other books than those mentioned.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I really don't understand the question. I've been reading all my life. And of course I absorbed all sorts of information from all sorts of sources, and it is certain that I have used my general knowledge from various books in various areas. But if you ask me about a specific book, whether I used it or not, I would be able to answer. It is difficult to enumerate all the books that I have used for making this report. I only quoted those which I quoted.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The next -- one of the next categories of sources that you used, as listed in paragraph 11 of your report, were transcripts of statements of witnesses.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You listed six individuals from the VRS whose witness statement transcripts you read. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can look up my own introduction. That's where I wrote it. I don't remember all the names, but yes. Lizdek, Sladoje, Lugonja, Sinkovic. I don't know the others, are there as well. Of course I quoted them. I've read them. And there's no reason for me to hide it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And witness, these transcripts that you read were from interviews that the Prosecution conducted with these individuals; is that right?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I received these copies from the Defence team. I don't know which form these interviews took. It was not my duty to deal with this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think in response to your last answer, you've answered this question, but were there -- from the transcripts that you were provided, did the Defence legal team indicate to you that you should read all of those transcripts?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. It was something that I asked for myself because I wanted to see what those people who were familiar with the situation said about the relevant period, because that is one of the criteria according to which I collected my information when preparing to draw up my report and come here to testify. I simply thought that this type of information should not be ignored because it is precious. And it would be with great satisfaction that I would read and use transcripts of testimonies of witnesses who are former BH army members, if only I had the opportunity.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, when you read these transcripts, do you recall seeing at the beginning of each of the transcripts questions where the person conducting the interview identified himself as an investigator with the Office of the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To be frank, I didn't pay attention to this particular line. I was more interested in the essence of the text. If I had paid attention, I would be able to give you a more certain answer.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You indicated -- you named the following individuals: Milanovic, Zarkovic, Indic, Lizdek, Sladoje, and Lugonja.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not Milanovic, Milovanovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Milovanovic. Are those the six individuals whose statement transcripts you recall reading?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think so, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you rely on information contained in those transcripts in producing your report?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not much. I rather used them as a secondary source than a primary one.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You also indicated that you relied on witness statement transcripts or witness statements from certain United Nations military observers or UNPROFOR personnel; is that right?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And again, you listed six or seven names and then specified others. Do you recall other than the names listed in paragraph 11 of your report which statements of which military observers or UNPROFOR personnel you read?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I really couldn't. If you could refresh my memory and remind me of a specific name, maybe I could say yes or no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you read a witness statement of Viktor Bezrouchenko?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, the documents that you've reviewed, you told us there's been at least 5.000 of them, and I think you also told us Thursday or Friday that it was tens of thousands of pages of documents. I'd like to focus your attention on the SRK documents that you reviewed. Where did you get those documents from?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I received SRK documents from the Defence.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Other than documents -- SRK documents received from the Defence, did you take any steps or efforts to obtain SRK documents from any other source?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The next source that you inform us you relied upon were the notes that you took of direct interviews - and I'm quoting your report - "with a series of outstanding superior officers of the SRK and direct participants in the war." You then indicated the functional titles of these individuals; is that right?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you rely on the information that you derived from these interviews in reaching the conclusions set forth in your report?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, except for certain locations and certain details that were not sufficiently clear to me from the documents. When I was reading the documents and studying the situation, some things seemed insufficiently clear and I wanted to clarify them, talking to the participants and looking at documentation of the 1st BH army Corps. So in order to find out more about this, to hear about these things from the participants, to get a more certain position, this information was important to me because it was firsthand information from people who directly participated in the war, although I didn't rely strictly upon it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. President, I note the time. Perhaps this would be an appropriate time for a break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll adjourn until ten minutes to 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ierace, you're on your feet.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. In relation to the videotape excerpt relevant to the evidence of Richard Gray, there was some homework to be done on the weekend by the Defence in relation to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Would you wish to deal with that, Mr. President, at the end of today's testimony perhaps?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Perhaps -- how much time would it take? Because there's another issue which takes perhaps one or a couple of minutes. I'd rather do it at the end so that we can then --

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- Excuse the witness for that moment. Mr. Mundis, would you please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, in your statement, you also indicated that you listened to audiotapes of the in-court testimony of certain witnesses that you considered relevant. You indicated UNMOs, UNPROFOR personnel, and three witnesses that you listed by name, Karavelic, Hadzic, and Zecevic. Did you listen to the audiotapes of the testimony of any other witnesses?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't understand. I mentioned those three --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I think there is a name, concerning the names. Could the Prosecution tell us where they found this claim, where this claim comes from.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. President, all of this information is contained in paragraph 11 of the report, in the English version pages 5 and 6. On page 6, you'll see about one-fourth of the way down "Audiotapes," and at the very end of the sentence -- or the paragraph with the word "audiotapes" underlined, you'll see those three names that I just mentioned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It says "et cetera."

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So it's not -- Mr. Piletta-Zanin, what is the problem? Yes, Ms. Pilipovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] To the extent that I followed the general's answer, Zecevic was not mentioned. That's why I asked my colleague to react. I think only Karavelic and Hadzic were mentioned, although the name is mentioned in the report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, the name is mentioned in the report. So that is a mistake then? You did not listen to the audio recording of the testimony of Mr. Zecevic, or did you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I watched the testimony of Mr. Zecevic when it was directly relayed on Belgrade television. It was broadcast live from the Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That's clear. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, after the name Zecevic, it says "et cetera." Can you tell us the names of any other witnesses who testified in this courtroom whose audiotape testimony you listened to in preparing your report?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, for example, I listened to Buha [as interpreted], Indic, and there were other witnesses too, but right now I can't remember the names. "Et cetera" means that the list is not complete. It means that I listened to other witnesses too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I ask you: Did you record somewhere what testimonies you have listened to? I mean, you say I don't remember, but is there some list where you did write down exactly what you heard?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I didn't write the names down. I listened to the tapes, I made a note of the facts that were important for me. These were working papers, the kind that anyone -- the kind of notes that anyone makes when working.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed, Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, the English transcript says that you listened to "Buha". Would that be Bukva?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Bukva, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall the names of any of the other members of the SRK whose testimony you listened to, besides Bukva and Indic?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not the names, but I do remember facts. I remember testimonies. For example, I watched the testimony which was broadcast live by a company commander from the Nedzarici Battalion, and then I also watched the live broadcast of the testimony of a witness from Grbavica, from the Jewish cemetery, and so on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: With respect to the testimony that you either watched the live broadcasts of or listened to the audiotapes of, can you please point us to any page or footnote in your report that refers to that testimony or that cites to that testimony for anything that you've written in your report.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I can't remember. I don't think that I cited this, because in my report such testimonies aren't of such importance for me to refer to unless it had to do with some specific position. But at the moment, right now I could not refer to anything -- specify anything in the report.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You told us, witness, or you wrote in paragraph 11, subparagraph 3 on page 6 that you made three study tours, each lasting four days to Sarajevo and its environs. You told us that a cameraman and a guide accompanied you on occasion. You were also joined by one of the chiefs of staff of one of the SRK brigades on one of those trips. Did anyone from the Defence legal team accompany you during any of these study trips?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mrs. Pilipovic was present, lead counsel.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was that on one of the study trips or all three of them?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't go on a single visit without being accompanied by Mrs. Pilipovic, lead counsel.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who was the SRK guide that accompanied you, and did that person accompany you on all the trips or simply one or two of them?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. President, could I avoid mentioning names in open session, if possible. If I have to mention names, I should appreciate it if we could go into private session. I simply wouldn't want to refer to names in any context whatsoever because I haven't obtained their consent to do so, if this is important.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: There's no objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Since the Prosecution has no objection, we'll turn into private session.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you take -- witness, did you take any notes of what this guide or guide --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that what preceded, that is to say, the difficulties the Defence had to carry out its interviews in a sort of fabricated anonymous way, I think that this should be incognito -- I don't think this should be in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Let me first -- Mr. Piletta-Zanin, the witness was responding to something not asked to him in this respect. He was asked about other things. On the other hand, I have no problem in -- you did not ask the witness about it during the examination-in-chief, but I have no problem in stating in open court that the witness, although that was not the subject of the questions said, that they used when visiting Sarajevo a relatively neutral car in order to prevent any -- any problems. And he said something about an electro company and that the cameraman had faced problems before. Please proceed, Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, did you take any notes of what these guides told you during any of these trips?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't use the guides. I didn't treat them as people with whom I would hold conversations. They escorted me. I asked them to take me to the locations that I had previously selected, and I believe that it wasn't important --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Excuse me. The question is: Did you take any notes from what these people told you when you were in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: spoke to him and I provided the notes I made about that conversation. I provided them to the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: While you were making your direct observation study trips, did you take any notes about what you saw during the time you were in Sarajevo making direct observations?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course, I did. And you have my notes on the video cassettes. I filmed the Sarajevo theatre, a panorama of Sarajevo from the viewpoint of the facilities used for the disposition of the units, to see what the disposition of both sides was, the deployment of both sides was, and this helped me to make the map.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I just say: You repeated the name you didn't want to pronounce in open session, so a redaction will be made in that respect. Yes? General Radinovic, you asked for closed session, and then in open session you repeated it. So could -- Madam Registrar, could perhaps the -- Yes. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't have that kind of caution, but I spoke to that person and I provided a note --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm not blaming you. But if you ask for private session, then please try to concentrate not to mention those information later on that you gave in private session. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, in response to the question, you said you have my notes on the video cassettes. Did you make any handwritten notes on paper or in a notebook or any other type of written notes while you were making your study trips to Sarajevo, notes of what you saw, what you could see from various locations, et cetera?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't write anything down.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, in addition to the videotape, did you take any still photographs at any time during your study trips to Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did anyone who was accompanying you take still photographs and did you rely on those still photographs in producing your report?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No one took any photographs in my team and in my presence, and I did not rely on photographs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In writing your report, did you rely on or did you review the videotape that you had made?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The video recordings that I shot? Is that what you're talking about?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The videotapes that were shot during your study visits, whether you took the video or someone else took the video, did you look at those videotapes when you were producing your report?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course. Several times.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you -- during the war, did you visit the Sarajevo theatre personally at any time during the war?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall in what capacity you visited the war -- or you visited Sarajevo during the war?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you please tell us what that capacity was.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said in the course of the examination-in-chief, in response to lead counsel, Mrs. Pilipovic, I said that in 1992 and 1993 I was the assistant to the Federal Ministry of Defence for strategy and for defence politics. At the same time, I was a military expert in our state delegation for the Geneva negotiations. And on each trip made by the prime minister of the government of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, I was a member of the delegation as a military expert. My trip to Sarajevo - I think it was at the end of July or the beginning of August, I can't remember exactly - it was with the delegation led by Milan Panic, the Yugoslav prime minister at the time. That was the first visit to Sarajevo. After the beginning of the war, he wanted to show symbolically that Yugoslavia wanted to put an end to the war, and I was in the column in which unfortunately the American reporter David Kaplan was killed. I'll remember that time, that event all my life. I joked with him in the plane, and I almost foresaw his death. So it's -- it's a sad memory.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, at the time, was this in July or August of 1992 or in 1993?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And as the military expert on the state delegation or assistant to the Federal Ministry of Defence for strategy, what were your specific duties and responsibilities?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On that trip to Sarajevo, I didn't have any. I just went there as someone who knew about armies and defence, and the prime minister Panic didn't go on a single trip without taking me with him because he thought if there were any subjects that would be of military interest, it would be good to have a military expert with him. We stayed in the UNPROFOR building and no military conversations of any kind were led, in particular -- were held in particular, apart from the fact that ...

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, at any time --

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Apart from the time that we sought for peace.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At any time after July or August of 1992 through the period August 1994 did you visit the city of Sarajevo for any other reason?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, unfortunately I didn't. I am emotionally tied to Sarajevo. I passed the exam to become a major in Sarajevo, so I am emotionally tied to Sarajevo. But that was my first trip and my only trip before preparing for this testimony.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, you wrote in your report that the study trips gave you the opportunity to learn some - and I'm quoting again - "significant empirical facts." Can you please point to a page or footnote in your report that refers to any of these facts which you learned as a result of your trip -- your study trips to Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Perhaps we view facts in a different way, we have different ideas of what facts are. I'll tell you what I thought about military facts: The position of the warring sides in the Sarajevo theatre are facts which are of key importance, and I visited these positions on foot and I became personally -- I personally saw what the tactical positions of those sides were. This was very important for me. I didn't have to cite anything. I told you how I determined the positions of both sides and how I obtained a view of the positions of the sides in the Sarajevo theatre. For me these are facts of key importance. Perhaps they're not such for you, but for me they are.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, these facts of key importance, where in your report do you cite or acknowledge the important facts which you personally observed during your trip to Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's in the part of my report that deals with the position of the forces of both sides and the analysis of the operative position of the 1st Corps and the Sarajevo Corps. But in particular, when they mention the elevations in the Sarajevo theatre, that was analysed in detail there, if you remember.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The question, witness, is: If I could find or if you could point me to a place where there's a footnote or words in the text to the effect that you discovered these facts on the basis of your study trips to Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't understand your question, in spite of my goodwill.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mundis would like to know what facts exactly are the result from your personal observation and where we find in your report that this fact or that fact is -- has become known to you as a result of your personal observation. I think Mr. Mundis is trying to identify what sources have played what role in your report.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'd have to provide you with a descriptive answer. I can't just say yes or no. When you pass by the Mojmilo Hill from the reservoir up to Grbavica, that is the best way to find out about the military facts that concern Mojmilo's military position, that is to say, to find out about the advantage that the side that has Mojmilo under its control has. It was only when I went there on foot that I saw this, although I was aware of Mojmilo, and then I had to write this down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me stop you. What Mr. Mundis seeks is where in your report you write the importance of -- "strategic importance of Mojmilo, I observed that with my own eyes during my visit." So he -- he's seeking for any reference to your personal visit, your personal observation, as the source of your -- of your opinion.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, in the introductory part where I wrote about my method and in order to make sure that the method was transparent, I described how I discovered the facts. If I had described each detail, every detail, the methodological part would have been longer than the report itself, which is fairly long. So I wasn't in a position to describe each detail. If I said that I visited that former front and the features held by the sides and that I observed positions on the spot, then that was a way of directly observing this. Should I have said this? Should I have stated this on each page, on every page? I don't think so. I mentioned this in the introduction. So that should have been sufficient.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Your answer is clear. You say "I gave a general reference to personal observation in my introduction and I've given my report, no more details." Please proceed, Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, when was your report completed?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A report of this kind is not completed once and for all. It is a process. There are as many methods as there are people. I have certainly made so far four or five different versions of this report. When I made the first draft, I was not happy either with the style or contents or the method of integration of various chapters, so I did it again. And the version that we now have in front of us was completed in November 2002. Maybe it was October. But there are -- there were several versions preceding it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, can you tell us where in the document you indicate the date that you completed the draft that was filed in November of 2002?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not think that this piece of information is important. It is a process of development. I didn't think it was important to write down when the first version was completed, and I just marked the date when my final one was done. You know, some works take 20 years to be written.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, there is no date specifying when you completed your report listed in your report; isn't that right? Yes or no?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think so. Maybe you can find out from context, but there are no dates because to me it is a totally insignificant fact.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You indicate, witness, at pages 5 and 6 that your expertise was completed before the military expertise of the Prosecution was completed.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You -- once the Prosecution military expertise was completed, you did not go back and revise your report, did you?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I finished this version too without looking at the military expertise of the Prosecution. I haven't received that military expertise to this day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me stop you there, witness. Did you ask the Defence legal team for the transcripts of the Prosecution military expertise?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course I did, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And they did not provide that to you for your use in producing your report?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They provided me with the materials submitted by Mr. Philipps, but that is not military expertise. That is the draft military structure of the SRK. I knew that even without the material from Mr. Philipps. I wanted to see how the Prosecution is analysing the military situation, the conduct of the warring sides. I wanted to see from that material if I had made a mistake that I could perceive only by comparing my military knowledge with the military knowledge of the Prosecution's expert. But I didn't receive that sort of military expertise, and unfortunately to this day after completing my report I still haven't got it. I didn't believe that such a major military problem can be treated without a serious military report from the other side. I think that this would be treated much better if we had two military experts, one on each side.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, do you know whether the documents or transcripts or any of the material that you relied upon in producing your report, if any of that material has actually been admitted into evidence?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I'm not on the Defence team, and I can't possibly know whether something is admitted into evidence or not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, you provided several weeks ago copies of the notes you took when you interviewed the individuals that you listed in your report as being superior members of the SRK. I'm going to ask now that the usher show you photocopies of those notes. There are several places, about nine places in the notes where our interpreters and translators have had a difficult time reading your handwriting, and I would like you to assist us by reading out what selected portions of your notes say. Do you understand what I'm asking you?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I understand what you're asking. But Your Honour, I want to ask this: Is it possible that every working draft is studied here? They were not made for this purpose. Of course I don't mind the Trial Chamber and the Prosecution reading my notes that I took over there, but I simply can't understand that such importance is attached to this sort of working paper, the notes that I took in the margin when talking to some people. It's just as when reading a book you make your own notes on the margin reflecting your impressions and immediate thoughts. But of course I will do whatever is asked of me. I simply think that it is hardly necessary. That was just one thing I did in preparation. It was one of the steps in my work.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: General Radinovic, the Prosecution wants to verify the sources you've used, and it is up to the parties to identify what they think to be important sources to verify and what not. So therefore, I'd like you to answer the questions in this respect, although I do understand that you find it not that relevant. But before doing so, are these longer -- how much time would it take, Mr. Mundis?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. President, we've got about -- or I have about nine of these excerpts. I do have a copy here where I've highlighted in the margins those portions which I'd like to witness to read out to us. I do not expect that we would finish this prior to breaking for today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But there is -- I think Mr. Ierace asked for a couple of minutes, Mr. Piletta-Zanin asked for some time. There are two ways of dealing with it: The first would be to start with it tomorrow; the other one would be to ask the witness whether on those specific parts indicated he could clarify the matter. But we also could do it tomorrow. It's just the way you want to use your time.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I make a suggestion, Your Honour, to save time?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous interpretation continues] ... Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am willing to offer my spare time to the Prosecutor to make whatever clarification if necessary, if it is not important to do it here in the courtroom. So in my spare time, I will be at their disposal to decipher whatever is unclear in my notes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. President, I think -- well, the Prosecution certainly appreciates the willingness of the expert to assist us. I think we would prefer that this material be read into the record. In the event he were to simply take the notes in an attempt to make them clear, we would still have problems with respect to translation. The notes as we currently have them have been translated and distributed to the parties and to the Bench. We would then have to revise that. It might actually take up more time than simply asking him to read short excerpts from these nine portions of the notes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then perhaps we will do that tomorrow morning and spend the time now on the -- Unless, there -- Mr. Ierace, how much time would you need?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Well, Mr. President, it's simply a matter of the Defence indicating if they've found the relevant passage and then what should follow from that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: In order to prevent that we -- in order to prevent that we are going to rush against the clock, we'd rather start with this exercise tomorrow, Mr. Mundis. If you would have one or two questions, then we could continue for just one or two minutes, but ...

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: I can certainly skip to another area and ask a few questions, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then would you please stop in three minutes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, the very first document that you were shown when you testified here, D246, clearly indicated that the JNA 4th Corps was renamed the Sarajevo Romanija Corps. It was essentially the old JNA 4th Corps under a new name. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Many units from the 4th Corps did not get transferred to the Sarajevo Romanija Corps. There is no mark of equality between the two.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. President, I would ask the witness be shown 246, the very first document shown on Thursday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Usher, would you please put it on the ELMO so that we ...

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, could you please read out what the main text of this document says.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The main part of this document speaks about the fact that the 4th Corps is renamed into Sarajevo Romanija Corps. And I wasn't disputing that. I just said that not all units of the 4th Corps ended up in the composition of the SRK, nor was the zone of responsibility of the 4th Corps turned into the zone of responsibility of the SRK. The brigade from Doboj is missing, another brigade --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Certainly, witness, the -- certainly the brigades, regiments, and battalions listed on that document were former 4th Corps subordinate units that were simply renamed and formed part of the Sarajevo Romanija Corps. That's what the document says.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: No further questions for today, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Mundis. General Radinovic, we will continue tomorrow morning at 9.00 in this same courtroom. We have to deal with one or two procedural issues. But meanwhile I ask Madam Usher to escort you out of the courtroom, and I'd like to instruct you not to speak with anyone about your testimony in this -- that you have given in this court or you're still about to give in this court. Yes? Thank you. And I hope to see you back tomorrow morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then I do understand, Mr. Ierace, you are waiting for a response of the review of the tapes over the weekend. Is there any response, Ms. Pilipovic? I'm talking about the Gray tapes, where to locate some sequences.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour -- Your Honour, I have to say that in the absence of my colleague, I reviewed three videotapes, two from the registry -- in fact, I think the third is two from the registry. I was confused by the fact that I don't have the original of the tapes, so I can't check that the recording corresponds to the original. The three videotapes that I have managed to see over the weekend contain certain excerpts from BBC programmes but very short. One of them is 49 minutes long or 39 minutes long, maybe even shorter, and the third videotape I believe contains no BBC programmes. So the fourth tape is still missing, and I do have to review it. I also received the videotape given by the Defence to the registry, a clerk gave it to me on Saturday, so I am still not able to compare the cassette disclosed by the Defence with parts of the original. The problem is, therefore, that I don't have the originals so that I can't see whether our own videotapes correspond to the originals. I believe that as far as the three tapes that I have so far managed to see are concerned, do not coincide with the original. I can't be very certain of this, but I believe that this is the problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Just to summarise. I do understand that you reviewed three videotapes. You did not identify on any of these three videotapes the sequences specifically referred to by the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I did not identify on any of these three tapes -- for instance, there was a sequence showing a radar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So you were not able -- and you still have to review the fourth tape; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Finally --

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But I think I don't have it. I don't think I have the fourth tape, but I'll look up my collection again because in the office where I'm working we have about 80 tapes. I didn't have numbers on the tapes I got from the registry, so I don't know if I have all four of them or only three. I'm not certain, because we got them in stages.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps there would -- if there's any doubt remaining, that by comparing at least how the tape starts, you could see whether these are the same tapes as the tapes that have meanwhile been received by the Prosecution. When can we expect that you have reviewed the fourth tape?

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I actually think I don't have the fourth tape. This afternoon I could try to contact my colleagues from the Prosecution so that we can identify the ones I've seen. I can tell them what the contents are and how they begin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So I expect that the Chamber will be informed tomorrow about the achievements made this afternoon. So we still do not know - I think I expressed myself in words - as to which party is most happy after the weekend. We still have to wait one more day to see who is the unhappy and who is the happier party. Is there anything else on this issue? Then, Mr. Piletta-Zanin, you asked for 30 seconds at the end of the hearing.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. Briefly, the Defence was not ready to question this witness. We say so and we say so in defence of our legitimate rights to prepare for a witness. From Friday, for reasons which are strictly personal and have to do with one of my relatives, I had a similar situation to the one which caused the suspension of this proceeding for several hours. I think you know what I'm talking about. I was asking for a -- I was asking for a suspension of the proceedings for several hours in order to be with them, and that was rejected. I didn't know until Sunday evening whether I would be able to attend until this morning, and this caused a major upheaval for the Defence because Mrs. Pilipovic didn't know whether she was supposed to take over -- to take over one part of the questioning which originally I planned to handle and for which I prepared and not she. I note that I made absolutely no comment on this matter. Another thing - and I am mustering the courage to tell you this - I formulated a request for recusal, and since then we are feeling an atmosphere here which is not pleasant. There are -- this is reflecting on everybody's quality of work, and I think this is hurting the presentation of the Defence case. I am saying the Defence case, because it is targeted against one person, certainly not Mr. Galic, and I think it is one of our functions to say things even if they are not pleasant. I tried to say this with the utmost respect but also with utmost clarity, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is there any need to respond, Mr. Ierace?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Well, Mr. President, I think in view of the last comment made by Mr. Piletta-Zanin, I should indicate as a matter of record that the Prosecution has not detected any change whatsoever in the attitude of the Bench towards the Defence or the Prosecution. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a moment, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you please use your microphone. It's not clear to me, Mr. Piletta-Zanin. You --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I'm watching the clock. We all have to abide by the clock. No comments for now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I do understand that you do not wish to make any comment at this moment. Then we'll adjourn until tomorrow morning, 9.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
